hypotheses.title: MetaQuantsFactory signatures lack per-signer/per-version replay protection
hypotheses.description: `_verifySignature` only checks `ECDSA.recover(toEthSignedMessageHash(updateData), signature) == signer` and does not bind the signature to a nonce, deadline, chain id, contract address, or to the requested version (`version` argument of `commit`). Any signed MetaQuants update payload is therefore a bearer token that can be replayed indefinitely across chains (same factory implementation deployed on Arbitrum/Optimism) and can be committed to any oracle version, including past/future timestamps within validFrom/validTo.
hypotheses.attackPath: 1. Observe a valid `(MetaQuantsUpdate encodedUpdate, signature)` pair for feed X. 2. Call `MetaQuantsFactory.commit([idX], version', data)` on the same chain or on any chain where the same signer is used, supplying the captured payload. 3. `_validatePrices` only checks `publishTime` is within `[version+validFrom, version+validTo]`, so the attacker picks a `version` whose bounded window contains publishTime. 4. `KeeperOracle.commit` stores the price as a valid request for that version on the attacker's schedule.
hypotheses.impact: Wrong prices injected into a market for chosen versions; attackers can force settlements at attacker-influenced prices, causing wrong PnL, liquidations, and loss of funds to traders/makers.
hypotheses.recommendation: Include version, chainid, and address(this) in the signed payload/EIP-712 typed data, and maintain a per-update nonce (or require a unique signer-provided commitment id) that is consumed on first use.

hypotheses.title: Chainlink price feed lacks staleness/round checks in KeeperFactory
hypotheses.description: `_parsePrices` decodes the verified Chainlink report and uses `observationsTimestamp` and `price` directly without checking `answeredInRound`, `updatedAt` freshness, or a minimum/maximum round. The only validation is `_validatePrices` in KeeperFactory, which checks the publish time against `version + validFrom/validTo` — but `validFrom`/`validTo` are owner-set and can be wide, and there is no check that the report is the latest round. A stale or out-of-order report can be committed as a valid price for a version.
hypotheses.attackPath: An attacker (anyone can call `KeeperFactory.commit`) submits an old but still-in-window Chainlink report for a requested version. `_validatePrices` passes because the timestamp is within `[version+validFrom, version+validTo]`. The stale price is stored as the version price and used to settle all positions, PnL, funding, and liquidations for that version.
hypotheses.impact: Wrong settlement prices cause incorrect PnL, funding, and liquidation decisions; attackers can profit by settling at a favorable stale price, and honest users can be liquidated incorrectly.
hypotheses.recommendation: Enforce that the report is the latest round (`answeredInRound >= roundId`), check `updatedAt` freshness against a max age, and reject zero/negative prices.

hypotheses.title: Pyth price feed accepts any publishTime within wide validFrom/validTo window
hypotheses.description: `_parsePrices` calls `pyth.parsePriceFeedUpdates` with `minPublishTime = type(uint64).min` and `maxPublishTime = type(uint64).max`, so Pyth itself performs no freshness check. The only freshness gate is `KeeperFactory._validatePrices`, which compares `publishTime` to `version + validFrom/validTo`. Since `validFrom`/`validTo` are owner-configurable and can be large, an attacker can commit an arbitrarily old Pyth price as long as it falls in the window.
hypotheses.attackPath: Attacker calls `KeeperFactory.commit` with a stale Pyth update whose `publishTime` is within `[version+validFrom, version+validTo]`. The stale price is accepted and used to settle the version, affecting PnL, funding, and liquidations.
hypotheses.impact: Stale price settlement leads to incorrect PnL/funding and potentially wrongful liquidations or profitable self-settlement.
hypotheses.recommendation: Pass tight `minPublishTime`/`maxPublishTime` bounds to `parsePriceFeedUpdates` derived from the version and a small max age, and reject prices older than that.

hypotheses.title: Pendings array allows any user to front-run victim's update with maxPending exhaustion
hypotheses.description: `_update` increments `context.global.currentId` whenever `context.currentTimestamp > updateContext.orderGlobal.timestamp`, and InvariantLib.validate reverts with `MarketExceedsPendingIdLimitError` when `context.global.currentId > context.global.latestId + maxPendingGlobal` (or the local equivalent). Because anyone may call `update(account, amount, referrer)` with `msg.sender` as signer via the 3-arg overload and the 4-arg `update(account, amount, collateral, referrer)`, an attacker can advance `currentId` repeatedly (each call opens a fresh pending id) without ever needing the victim's authorization. Since the victim's own `update`/`settle` shares the same `global.currentId` window, the attacker can fill up to `maxPendingGlobal` pending orders belonging to random accounts, freezing the victim's settle/withdraw path until the oracle commits the pending versions.
hypotheses.attackPath: 1) Attacker observes a victim account about to withdraw. 2) Attacker calls `market.update(victim, 0, referrer)` with `msg.sender == victim`? No—attacker instead calls `update(attacker, 0, attackerReferrer)` repeatedly across many fresh accounts/timestamps, each advancing `global.currentId` one slot. 3) Once `currentId == latestId + maxPendingGlobal`, any legitimate update by *any* user reverts with `MarketExceedsPendingIdLimitError`. 4) Settlement of pending orders depends on oracle commits; until those land the market cannot be advanced.
hypotheses.impact: Legitimate users cannot settle, update, or withdraw their collateral until the oracle advances versions (which itself requires keepers to be incentivized and willing). Funds are effectively locked in the interim and any pending withdrawal is DoS'd.
hypotheses.recommendation: Charge a meaningful anti-spam cost (e.g., require nonzero collateral or a valid operator/signer signature) for opening new pending ids, or make the pending-id limit per-account rather than shareable across all senders in this window.

hypotheses.title: Vault._settleUnderlying loops all markets; one failing market bricks the vault
hypotheses.description: `_settleUnderlying` iterates `market.settle(address(this))` for every registered market without try/catch. Any market that reverts in `settle` (e.g., because of `MarketStalePriceError`, a poisoned pending order, or `VersionStorageLib.store` overflow as described elsewhere) causes every Vault entrypoint that calls `_settleUnderlying` — `settle`, `rebalance`, `update`, `_maxDeposit`, `register`, `updateWeights`, `updateLeverage`, `updateParameter` — to revert. Because markets are added by the owner and the vault rebalances through them, a single compromised or bugged registered market freezes all vault deposits, redemptions, and rebalances.
hypotheses.attackPath: Attacker finds or creates a Market satisfying `Vault` registration (through the registry) whose `settle` can be made to revert — for instance, a market with `staleAfter = 0` and a stale oracle, or the poisoned-pending scenario above. Since vault markets are per-vault but the attacker can induce `settle` reverts on any already-registered market (via the same pending-order DoS), the vault becomes unusable.
hypotheses.impact: User deposits and redemptions are permanently blocked; the vault's shares/asset accounting is unreachable and collateral is stuck in the underlying markets.
hypotheses.recommendation: Wrap each market's `settle` in a try/catch, skip failed markets for the current operation, and record the failure so users can still redeem at the last known checkpoint.

hypotheses.title: _updateIntent charges solver's settlement fee to the wrong signer due to order invalidation
hypotheses.description: In `update(Intent, signature)`/`update(Fill,...)` the solver side is settled by calling `_updateIntent(account, msg.sender, intent.amount.neg(), ...)` where `account` comes from the caller (solver) and `signer` is `msg.sender`. The intent's `common.signer` is used only for verification; `_loadForUpdate` then calls `MarketFactory.authorization(context.account, msg.sender, signer, orderReferrer)` with `account = solver`. Any external solver can therefore pay their own account while the signed intent declares a different `common.account`; the on-chain accounting for the trade fee and referral attribution is derived from the wrong signer (msg.sender), not `intent.common.signer`.
hypotheses.attackPath: 1. Attacker listens for a signed `Intent` (or `Fill`) from a victim. 2. Attacker calls `market.update(attackerEOA, intent, signature)` so `intent.common.account` in the passed intent differs from the attacker's address. 3. `_updateIntent(account=attacker, signer=msg.sender=attacker, amount=-intent.amount, ...)` executes the solver side on the attacker's local and `updateContext.signer` is the attacker, not the declared signer. 4. The solver-referral fee `solverReferralFee` is loaded via `authorization(account=attacker, ...)`.
hypotheses.impact: Solver referral fees, trade fees, and per-account state can be manipulated to shift value between accounts; the intent is executed without the correct account identity being enforced for the solver side.
hypotheses.recommendation: Require `intent.common.signer == msg.sender` (or `intent.common.account == account`) in `_updateIntent`, and pass `intent.common.signer` (not `msg.sender`) into the solver side so signer-based attribution and fee splits use the signed identity.

hypotheses.title: MetaQuantsFactory accepts signed updates with no timestamp freshness check
hypotheses.description: `_parsePrices` verifies the signer's signature over `encodedUpdate` and decodes `publishTime`, but never checks that `publishTime` is recent or matches the requested version. The only check is `KeeperFactory._validatePrices` against `version + validFrom/validTo`. Because the signer is a single trusted key and updates are replayable, an attacker can resubmit an old signed update whose `publishTime` still falls in the window.
hypotheses.attackPath: Attacker replays a previously signed MetaQuants update (or one with an old `publishTime`) via `KeeperFactory.commit`. `_validatePrices` passes if the timestamp is in the window, and the stale price is committed for the version.
hypotheses.impact: Stale price settlement causes incorrect PnL/funding and can be exploited for wrongful liquidations or favorable self-settlement.
hypotheses.recommendation: Require `publishTime` to be within a tight bound of `version` (e.g., `version <= publishTime <= version + maxAge`) and reject updates whose timestamp is older than the latest committed version.

hypotheses.title: VersionLib._accumulateSettlementFee underflows when guarantee.orders > order.orders
hypotheses.description: `uint256 orders = context.order.orders - context.guarantee.orders;` is unchecked subtraction on unsigned integers. `GuaranteeLib.from` sets `newGuarantee.orders = order.orders`, and `OrderLib.add` accumulates both, so in normal flow they match. However, `OrderLib.invalidate` zeroes `order.orders` while leaving `guarantee.orders` intact, and `_processOrderGlobal` calls `newOrder.invalidate(newGuarantee)` before `VersionLib.accumulate`. If the order is invalidated, `order.orders == 0` while `guarantee.orders > 0`, causing an underflow revert that blocks settlement of that version.
hypotheses.attackPath: An attacker submits an intent whose oracle version is invalid (e.g. by committing an invalid price via the keeper factory, or by exploiting the timeout path in `_commitRequested` which sets `valid = false`). The order is invalidated, `order.orders` becomes 0, and `_accumulateSettlementFee` underflows, permanently bricking settlement for that market version.
hypotheses.impact: Market settlement DoS; funds frozen in the market until governance intervention.
hypotheses.recommendation: Guard the subtraction: `uint256 orders = context.order.orders > context.guarantee.orders ? context.order.orders - context.guarantee.orders : 0;`.

hypotheses.title: CheckpointLib._accumulateSettlementFee underflow on invalidated orders
hypotheses.description: Same pattern as VersionLib: `uint256 orders = order.orders - guarantee.orders;` is unchecked. When `OrderLib.invalidate` is called (invalid oracle version), `order.orders` is zeroed but `guarantee.orders` retains its value, so the subtraction underflows and reverts. This blocks `_processOrderLocal` and therefore account settlement.
hypotheses.attackPath: Attacker triggers an invalid oracle version (e.g. via the timeout path in `KeeperOracle._commitRequested` where `valid = false`), causing `newOrder.invalidate(newGuarantee)` in `_processOrderLocal`. The subsequent `CheckpointLib.accumulate` reverts on underflow, freezing the account's settlement.
hypotheses.impact: Account settlement DoS; user funds frozen.
hypotheses.recommendation: Use saturating subtraction or check `order.orders >= guarantee.orders` before subtracting.

hypotheses.title: TriggerOrder.canExecute uses latest oracle price without staleness check
hypotheses.description: `canExecute` checks `latestVersion.valid` and compares `latestVersion.price` to the trigger price, but does not check that `latestVersion.timestamp` is recent. If the oracle is stale (e.g., no keeper has committed for a while), `latest()` returns the last committed version, which may be old. A trigger order can be executed against a stale price that no longer reflects the market.
hypotheses.attackPath: Attacker waits for the oracle to become stale, then calls `Manager.executeOrder` on a trigger order whose condition is satisfied by the stale price. The order executes at the stale price, and the attacker profits from the price discrepancy when the oracle catches up.
hypotheses.impact: Trigger orders execute at stale prices, causing losses to the order owner and profits to the attacker.
hypotheses.recommendation: In `canExecute`, require `block.timestamp - latestVersion.timestamp <= maxStaleAfter` (or a similar freshness bound) before allowing execution.

hypotheses.title: MultiInvoker._executeOrder uses stale pending position without freshness check
hypotheses.description: `_executeOrder` calls `canExecuteOrder` (which uses `market.oracle().latest()` without a staleness check), then `_marketSettle`, then reads `market.pendings(account)` and `market.positions(account)` to compute the new position. If the oracle is stale, the trigger condition may be satisfied by an old price, and the order executes against a stale market state. The `_update` call then submits a new order that will settle at the next (possibly much different) price.
hypotheses.attackPath: Attacker waits for the oracle to become stale, then calls `MultiInvoker.invoke` with `EXEC_ORDER` for a trigger order whose condition is satisfied by the stale price. The order executes, and the attacker profits when the oracle updates.
hypotheses.impact: Trigger orders execute at stale prices, causing losses to the order owner and profits to the attacker.
hypotheses.recommendation: Add a staleness check in `canExecuteOrder` (or in `_executeOrder`) that rejects execution if `block.timestamp - latestVersion.timestamp > maxStaleAfter`.

hypotheses.title: Manager.executeOrder charges interface fee before order execution, allowing fee on unexecuted order
hypotheses.description: `executeOrder` calls `_chargeInterfaceFee(market, account, order)` before `order.execute(market, account)`. `_chargeInterfaceFee` calls `controller.chargeFee(account, feeAmount)` which pulls DSU from the collateral account. If `order.execute` subsequently reverts (e.g., market update fails due to margin, stale price, or market paused), the entire transaction reverts, so no loss. However, `_chargeInterfaceFee` computes `feeAmount` using `order.notionalValue(market, account)` which reads `market.oracle().latest()` and the account's current position. Between the fee charge and the execution, `order.execute` calls `market.settle(account)` and `market.update`, which can change the position and price. The fee is thus computed on a stale position/price, and the keeper fee is raised after execution using `_handleKeeperFee` with `keepConfigBuffered`. More critically, `_chargeInterfaceFee` is called before `order.isSpent = true` is stored, so if `controller.chargeFee` triggers a callback (e.g., via DSU token hooks or reserve interactions) that re-enters `executeOrder` for the same order, the order is not yet marked spent and can be executed twice.
hypotheses.attackPath: 1. Attacker places a trigger order with an interface fee whose receiver is a contract that, upon receiving DSU via `controller.chargeFee`, re-enters `Manager.executeOrder` for the same `(market, account, orderId)`. 2. First call: `_chargeInterfaceFee` pulls DSU, triggering the receiver's callback. 3. Callback re-enters `executeOrder`; `checkOrder` still sees `isSpent == false`, so it proceeds, charges the interface fee again, and executes the order. 4. Both executions apply the order delta, doubling the position change and double-charging the interface fee.
hypotheses.impact: Double execution of trigger order, double position change, double interface fee charge, and potential under-margining or loss of funds.
hypotheses.recommendation: Set `order.isSpent = true` and store it before calling `_chargeInterfaceFee` and `order.execute`, or add a reentrancy guard to `executeOrder`.

hypotheses.title: MultiInvoker executeOrder raises fee from account before executing, reverts if account lacks DSU
hypotheses.description: `_executeOrder` calls `_handleKeeperFee` (which invokes `_raiseKeeperFee`) *before* `_marketSettle` and the actual position update. `_raiseKeeperFee` calls `_marketWithdraw(market, account, raisedKeeperFee)` which invokes `market.update(account, MAX, MAX, MAX, -raisedKeeperFee, false)` — an act that both requires the account to remain solvent after withdrawal and charges a market trade/settlement fee. If the victim's account is close to liquidation margin, the withdrawal for the keeper fee causes `InvariantLib.validate` to revert (`MarketInsufficientMarginError` / `MarketInsufficientCollateralError`), reverting the entire execution. Anyone (including the victim's adversary) can thus prevent a pending trigger order from executing simply by ensuring the account is near margin, because the keeper-fee withdrawal is mandatory and reverts the whole tx.
hypotheses.attackPath: 1) Victim places a trigger order with `maxFee > 0`. 2) Attacker pushes/keeps victim near their margin (e.g., by dust-poking the market price or by triggering another position update on behalf of the victim via signed intent). 3) When the trigger condition becomes true, anyone attempting `executeOrder` reverts due to the pre-execute fee withdrawal violating margin. The trigger order never lands, allowing the attacker to avoid a stop-loss/liquidation-avoidance fill.
hypotheses.impact: Trigger orders cannot execute near margin, defeating the primary use case (auto-close / risk management) and potentially causing the account to be liquidated at worse terms.
hypotheses.recommendation: Perform the keeper-fee raise after the position update succeeds (or cap it against what the resulting account can sustain), or route the fee through a separate accounting path that does not require a full market update.

hypotheses.title: Verifier._authorized accepts any market factory signer for any domain
hypotheses.description: `Verifier._authorized` returns true if `marketFactory.signers(account, signer)` is set, without cross-checking that the message domain matches the account being signed for. Because `MarketFactory.updateSigner` allows an account to enable any signer and `Verifier.verify*` messages include `domain` only in the hash (not gated), any signer authorized by account A can sign messages with `common.account = A` for any market/domain; combined with the fact that a signer is not otherwise scoped, a compromised or malicious delegated signer can produce signed intents/takes/updates for any market instance that consumes the same Verifier.
hypotheses.attackPath: 1. Victim enables a signer S to sign orders on market M. 2. Attacker (or the signer itself, if it is a contract/EOA that gains a compromise) constructs a `Take` with `common.account = victim`, `common.domain = M2` (any other market using the same Verifier). 3. Attacker calls `M2.update(take, sig)`; Verifier passes because `marketFactory.signers(victim, S)` is true. 4. M2 executes the take against the victim's account.
hypotheses.impact: A single authorized signer can move positions/collateral on any market the victim has authorized the signer for, not just the intended market, breaking signer scope.
hypotheses.recommendation: In `_authorized`, require that the signing domain matches the calling market (or that signer scoping is per (account, domain)), e.g. check `signers[account][domain][signer]` or pass the market address and require `signer` enablement is per-market.

hypotheses.title: KeeperFactory.commit is unrestricted; any caller can commit prices
hypotheses.description: `commit` is `external payable` with no access control. Any caller passes `oracleIds`, `version`, `data` and `msg.value`. Intent is that the caller is a keeper who parses/pays Pyth/Chainlink. `_parsePrices` in `PythFactory`/`ChainlinkFactory` forwards `msg.value` to Chainlink/Pyth to pay oracle update fees. The caller can choose any valid data so long as `_validatePrices` (validFrom/validTo window) passes. This means any unauthorised caller can commit a valid but arbitrarily-near version and receive keeper compensation from the market (pushed to `msg.sender`) via `KeeperOracle.commit(...)`. The keeper fee (settlementFee pushed) even if data.length==0 is still paid out via `_commitRequested` when `block.timestamp <= next()+timeout` uses the invalid-data path, meaning a caller can call `commit(ids, version, "")` to force a 0-price commit that is stored and pays a sync fee from the market's token to the caller.
hypotheses.attackPath: 1) Pick any registered `oracleId`. 2) Call `commit([oracleId], next(), "")` with empty data. 3) `_commitRequested` runs (`block.timestamp <= next()+timeout`), reads previous price, marks valid=false, computes syncFee, stores, `_global.latestIndex++`. 4) Back in `KeeperOracle.commit`, `market.token().push(receiver=msg.sender, syncFee)` pays the attacker from market token (collateral). That drain is real if push is not funded by the caller.
hypotheses.impact: Draining of market collateral via repeated zero-data commits; also invalid oracle versions get recorded.
hypotheses.recommendation: Require `data.length > 0` for the fee-paying path or require the caller to pay syncFee themselves; only push fees when data was provided and valid.
